subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 22-year-old woman has a pruritic, scaly, annular rash on her forearm. Skin scrapings are treated with potassium hydroxide (KOH) and a blue fungal stain; microscopy reveals branching septate hyphae. She recently acquired a new kitten.
question: Which of the following groups of organisms most likely produced these findings?

options.text: Malassezia species showing spaghetti-and-meatballs forms on KOH
Candida albicans showing budding yeast and pseudohyphae
Dermatophytes (Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton) showing branching septate hyphae
Bartonella species showing pleomorphic gram-negative rods
Herpes simplex virus showing multinucleated giant cells

explanation_correct: Tinea refers to cutaneous fungal infections caused by dermatophytes, primarily Microsporum, Trichophyton, and Epidermophyton. These fungi appear as branching septate hyphae on KOH preparation with blue fungal stain, and infection is associated with pruritus. This patient's scaly annular lesion, kitten exposure, and septate hyphae on KOH are classic for a dermatophyte infection. Malassezia is a yeastlike fungus with a different microscopy appearance, and the other options are not dermatophytes.

explanation_incorrect.A: Malassezia causes tinea versicolor and shows spaghetti-and-meatballs forms on KOH, not branching septate hyphae, and it is not a dermatophyte.
explanation_incorrect.B: Candida albicans shows budding yeast with pseudohyphae and typically causes mucosal or systemic infection, not the branching septate hyphae of dermatophytes.
explanation_incorrect.D: Bartonella is a bacterium causing bacillary angiomatosis with neutrophilic capillary papules, not a fungus visible on KOH.
explanation_incorrect.E: Herpes simplex virus produces multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear, not branching septate hyphae on KOH.

educationalObjective: Dermatophytes (Microsporum, Trichophyton, Epidermophyton) cause tinea and appear as branching septate hyphae on KOH with blue fungal stain.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Dermatology: Cutaneous mycoses

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 6-year-old boy has several scaly, erythematous patches on his scalp with areas of hair loss. He has tender cervical lymphadenopathy. KOH examination of scalp scrapings shows branching septate hyphae, and a Wood lamp examination shows fluorescence of some hairs.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tinea capitis
Tinea corporis
Tinea cruris
Tinea pedis
Alopecia areata

explanation_correct: Tinea capitis is a dermatophyte infection of the scalp that produces scaling, alopecia, and often lymphadenopathy, matching this child's presentation. KOH shows branching septate hyphae, and some Microsporum species fluoresce under Wood lamp. It is common in children. The other tinea subtypes involve different body sites, and alopecia areata is a noninfectious autoimmune alopecia without scale, hyphae, or lymphadenopathy.

explanation_incorrect.B: Tinea corporis occurs on the body, usually the torso, with annular scaly rings and central clearing, not a scalp infection with alopecia and lymphadenopathy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Tinea cruris is a dermatophyte infection of the inguinal region (jock itch), not the scalp.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tinea pedis is a dermatophyte infection of the feet (athlete's foot), not the scalp.
explanation_incorrect.E: Alopecia areata causes painless, well-demarcated hair loss without scale, hyphae on KOH, or cervical lymphadenopathy.

educationalObjective: Tinea capitis is a scalp dermatophyte infection with scaling, alopecia, and lymphadenopathy.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 34-year-old man has an enlarging, erythematous, scaly ring on his forearm with noticeable central clearing. He recently adopted a puppy. KOH examination shows branching septate hyphae. He asks how this differs from the jock itch his brother has in the groin.
question: Which of the following best identifies his infection and its distinguishing feature?

options.text: Tinea cruris, a groin infection that typically shows prominent central clearing
Tinea capitis with scaling and alopecia of the scalp
Tinea pedis with interdigital scaling of the feet
Tinea versicolor with hypopigmented patches on the trunk
Tinea corporis, an enlarging scaly ring with central clearing, often acquired from infected pets or farm animals; tinea cruris often lacks central clearing

explanation_correct: Tinea corporis (ringworm) occurs on the body, usually the torso or extremities, and is characterized by enlarging erythematous, scaly rings with central clearing. It can be acquired from contact with infected pets or farm animals, as with this patient's puppy. Tinea cruris occurs in the inguinal region (jock itch) and often does not show the central clearing typical of tinea corporis. This patient's annular scaly plaque with central clearing and pet exposure fits tinea corporis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Tinea cruris occurs in the groin and often lacks central clearing; it is not an annular plaque with central clearing on the forearm.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tinea capitis involves the scalp with alopecia and lymphadenopathy, not a scaly annular plaque on the forearm.
explanation_incorrect.C: Tinea pedis involves the feet, most commonly in an interdigital distribution, not the forearm.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tinea versicolor produces hypopigmented or pink patches from Malassezia, not an annular scaly plaque with central clearing.

educationalObjective: Tinea corporis is an annular scaly plaque with central clearing acquired from pets or farm animals; tinea cruris often lacks central clearing.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 19-year-old athlete has itchy, peeling, white macerated skin between his toes, along with a diffuse scaly moccasin-distribution rash over the sole of one foot. He uses communal showers. KOH examination of scale shows branching septate hyphae.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this condition?

options.text: A Malassezia yeast infection with spaghetti-and-meatballs forms on KOH
A dermatophyte infection of the foot (athlete's foot) with interdigital, moccasin, and vesicular varieties
A Candida albicans infection with budding yeast and pseudohyphae
A poxvirus infection producing umbilicated papules
A staphylococcal infection of the superficial epidermis with honey-colored crusts

explanation_correct: Tinea pedis (athlete's foot) is a dermatophyte infection of the feet with three varieties: interdigital (the most common), moccasin distribution, and vesicular. This athlete's interdigital maceration and moccasin-pattern scale, plus branching septate hyphae on KOH, are classic. Communal showers are a common source. The other options describe organisms or morphologies not consistent with a dermatophyte foot infection.

explanation_incorrect.A: Malassezia causes tinea versicolor with hypopigmented patches and spaghetti-and-meatballs forms, not interdigital or moccasin foot rash.
explanation_incorrect.C: Candida albicans shows budding yeast and pseudohyphae and typically causes mucosal disease, not this dermatophyte foot eruption.
explanation_incorrect.D: A poxvirus causes molluscum contagiosum with umbilicated papules, not a scaly interdigital rash with hyphae.
explanation_incorrect.E: Staphylococcal superficial infection produces impetigo with honey-colored crusts, not a scaly dermatophyte foot infection with hyphae.

educationalObjective: Tinea pedis is a dermatophyte foot infection with interdigital, moccasin, and vesicular patterns.
source: Generated from 11. Musculoskeletal.pdf - Dermatology: Cutaneous mycoses

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 62-year-old man has thickened, yellow, brittle toenails with subungual debris that have gradually worsened over 2 years. He has a history of athlete's foot. KOH examination of a nail scraping shows branching septate hyphae.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tinea versicolor
Tinea capitis
Psoriasis with nail pitting
Tinea unguium (onychomycosis), a dermatophyte infection of the nails
Traumatic onycholysis without infection

explanation_correct: Tinea unguium, also called onychomycosis, is a dermatophyte infection of the nails. It causes thickened, yellow, brittle nails with subungual debris, often in patients with a history of tinea pedis. The branching septate hyphae on KOH of nail scrapings confirm a dermatophyte. The other options do not produce septate hyphae on KOH or this combination of nail findings.

explanation_incorrect.A: Tinea versicolor is a Malassezia infection producing hypopigmented trunk patches with spaghetti-and-meatballs forms, not infected nails.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tinea capitis is a scalp dermatophyte infection with alopecia and lymphadenopathy, not a nail infection.
explanation_incorrect.C: Psoriasis can cause nail pitting, but it would not show branching septate hyphae on KOH of nail scrapings.
explanation_incorrect.E: Traumatic onycholysis causes nail detachment without septate hyphae on KOH or the typical yellowish subungual debris of onychomycosis.

educationalObjective: Tinea unguium (onychomycosis) is a dermatophyte nail infection with thickened, yellow, brittle nails and hyphae on KOH.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 24-year-old man develops multiple hypopigmented, finely scaly patches on his upper trunk during the summer. The areas fail to darken with sun exposure. KOH microscopy of scale shows short hyphae and round yeast forms described as spaghetti and meatballs. He is otherwise healthy and is less pruritic than patients with ringworm.
question: Which of the following best explains the pathogenesis and treatment of this condition?

options.text: Malassezia, a yeastlike fungus that is not a dermatophyte, degrades lipids into acids that inhibit tyrosinase, causing hypopigmentation; KOH shows spaghetti-and-meatballs forms and treatment includes selenium sulfide
A dermatophyte with branching septate hyphae that invades keratin and is treated with selenium sulfide
Tinea corporis with central clearing acquired from an infected animal
Vitiligo from autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, treated with topical corticosteroids
Candida albicans infection treated with oral fluconazole

explanation_correct: Tinea (pityriasis) versicolor is caused by Malassezia species, a yeastlike fungus that is not a dermatophyte despite its name. Lipid degradation by the organism produces acids that inhibit tyrosinase, reducing melanin synthesis and causing hypopigmentation; hyperpigmented or pink patches can also occur from inflammation. KOH shows the characteristic spaghetti-and-meatballs appearance (short hyphae plus round yeast cells), and treatment includes selenium sulfide and topical or oral antifungals. It is more common in hot, humid weather and is less pruritic than dermatophyte infections.

explanation_incorrect.B: Dermatophytes produce branching septate hyphae and cause tinea infections with central clearing, not the spaghetti-and-meatballs forms of Malassezia, and selenium sulfide is not the standard dermatophyte therapy described here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Tinea corporis is a dermatophyte infection with annular scaly plaques and central clearing, not the hypopigmented patches and spaghetti-and-meatballs forms of tinea versicolor.
explanation_incorrect.D: Vitiligo is autoimmune melanocyte destruction with depigmented macules and no fungal forms on KOH; it is not treated with selenium sulfide.
explanation_incorrect.E: Candida albicans shows budding yeast with pseudohyphae and causes mucosal or systemic disease, not the hypopigmented, spaghetti-and-meatballs eruption described here.

educationalObjective: Tinea versicolor is a non-dermatophyte Malassezia yeast infection; lipid-derived acids inhibit tyrosinase causing hypopigmentation, KOH shows spaghetti-and-meatballs, and selenium sulfide is treatment.
